data.burns_note: Found where NASA's reconstruction leaves the force model by more than 0.05 m/s in half an hour, up to the arrival at the Moon; each is shown as one instant. A burn in a gap of the reconstruction is not seen. Burns in lunar orbit are not listed: there the force model and the reconstruction part by about 1 m/s at each close pass of the Moon, as much as a small burn.

corrections.label: A budget for these errors, not a prediction of what the mission needed. The accuracy published in the user’s guide for Falcon 9 Block 5 is used for the errors at leaving Earth that it covers, worked out from its row for a transfer orbit to geosynchronous orbit, because the guide has no row for a launch to the Moon. Every other error is assumed.

assumptions.source: Falcon 9 Launch Vehicle Payload User’s Guide, Rev 2 (21 October 2015), Table 3-2, page 16; row: Geosynchronous transfer orbit (185 km x 35,786 km). The guide has no row for a launch to the Moon, so its row for a transfer orbit to geosynchronous orbit is used in its place. The orbit’s lowest point within 10 km at three standard deviations, so one standard deviation is 3.3 km.

assumptions.source: Falcon 9 Launch Vehicle Payload User’s Guide, Rev 2 (21 October 2015), Table 3-2, page 16; row: Geosynchronous transfer orbit (185 km x 35,786 km). The guide has no row for a launch to the Moon, so its row for a transfer orbit to geosynchronous orbit is used in its place. The orbit’s highest point within 500 km at three standard deviations. The speed error at the lowest point that would move the highest point that far is 2.7 m/s at one standard deviation, taken as the same at leaving Earth for the Moon.

Falcon 9 Launch Vehicle Payload User’s Guide, Rev 2 (21 October 2015), Table 3-2, page 16; row: Geosynchronous transfer orbit (185 km x 35,786 km). The guide has no row for a launch to the Moon, so its row for a transfer orbit to geosynchronous orbit is used in its place. The orbit’s tilt within 0.1° at three standard deviations. The sideways speed error at the lowest point that would tilt it that far is 6.0 m/s at one standard deviation, taken as the same at leaving Earth for the Moon.

corrections.plan_note: The flight as planned: NASA's reconstruction just before entering lunar orbit, propagated back to where it passed closest to Earth (5,390 km up, 8 min after the flown departure). Forward from there it arrives where and when the flown one did, with no burn on the way.
corrections.flown_note: The reconstruction shows corrections of 1.15 m/s after leaving Earth (any in its gaps are not seen).

belt_hours.source: Inside the belts: where the maps hold electrons above 1 MeV or protons above 10 MeV. AE8/AP8 MAX (IRBEM): the year before averaged 155 sunspots a day, against 2 to 155 over the 11 years before (OMNI), so the solar-maximum maps. NASA's reconstruction starts 4,769 km above Earth, so the climb out of the parking orbit before it is not counted: a lower bound.

electron_fluence_gt1mev.source: AE8/AP8 MAX (IRBEM): the year before averaged 155 sunspots a day, against 2 to 155 over the 11 years before (OMNI), so the solar-maximum maps. The solar-minimum maps give 1.4e+10.

fluence_gt10mev.source: Trapped protons above 10 MeV. AE8/AP8 MAX (IRBEM): the year before averaged 155 sunspots a day, against 2 to 155 over the 11 years before (OMNI), so the solar-maximum maps. The solar-minimum maps give 7.9e+08.

gcr_dose_mgy_day.source: From 18.9 cGy a year in silicon, measured by CRaTER's microdosimeter on LRO on 20 June 2009, about 10,000 km from the Moon (Mazur et al. 2011, as given by Schwadron et al. 2012, JGR 117, E00H13), scaled by the cosmic-ray model's change between then (W = 5) and 2025-01 (W = 108): ×0.33 (Matthiä et al. 2013, W from the Oulu neutron monitor, NMDB). ±30 % covers the scaling.

open_sky.no_margin_reason: A flat horizon, assumed: the elevation model does not cover this site.

gcr_dose_mgy_day.source: From 13.2 ± 1 µGy an hour in silicon, measured on the surface by Chang'e-4's LND from January 2019 (Zhang et al. 2020, Science Advances 6, eaaz1334), its horizon taken as flat, scaled by the cosmic-ray model's change between then (W = 16) and 2025-03 (W = 105): ×0.37 (Matthiä et al. 2013, W from the Oulu neutron monitor, NMDB). ±30 % covers the scaling. Times the site's open sky (1.000).

radiation.surface_note: The elevation model does not cover this landing site, so its horizon is taken as flat (open sky 1); the surface dose is an assumption to that extent.
radiation.sep_note: One solar particle event crossed NOAA's threshold (10 pfu above 10 MeV at GOES) during the trip, from NASA DONKI; its fluence is not worked out.

fluence_gt10mev.no_margin_reason: As measured at 1 AU outside Earth's magnetic field (taken as arriving evenly from all directions); GOES proton detector, 5-minute averages (NOAA NCEI), 1989-10-19 12:00 to 1989-11-01 00:00 UTC; peak 42,200 pfu above 10 MeV (NOAA's list: 40,000).

As measured at 1 AU outside Earth's magnetic field (taken as arriving evenly from all directions); GOES proton detector, 5-minute averages (NOAA NCEI), 2003-10-28 11:00 to 2003-11-01 00:00 UTC; peak 29,500 pfu above 10 MeV (NOAA's list: 29,500).

As measured at 1 AU outside Earth's magnetic field (taken as arriving evenly from all directions); King (1974), J. Spacecraft Rockets 11, 401: fitted spectrum J(>E) = 7.9e9 exp((30 - E)/26.5) per cm², as SPENVIS gives it.

radiation.screening_note: Screening only: long-term average belt maps (good to about a factor of two), cosmic-ray dose scaled from measurements (±30 %), and past events as they were measured at 1 AU. None of it accounts for the spacecraft's own shielding. Confirm in SPENVIS, OLTARIS or CREME-MC before any design decision.

parts.note: A screening estimate: belt maps good to about a factor of two, cosmic-ray dose ±30 %; confirm in SPENVIS, OLTARIS or CREME-MC.
NASA's reconstruction as archived; its own accuracy is not published with it.
Spherical Earth and Moon; the ± on sunlight and the longest shadow is the change when Earth's shadow is made 2 % larger for its atmosphere.
A station 'can see' the spacecraft when it is above the station's mask; antenna pointing and bookings are not modelled.
